Alert on __init__.py files with obfuscated code, network connections, or subprocess spawning within package initialization. Baseline package installation signatures against official PyPI artifacts.

suggestion.title: Detect CVE-2021-27137 DD-WRT Buffer Overflow Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article states C0XMO is 'delivered by exploiting CVE-2021-27137, a buffer overflow vulnerability caused by insufficient user input' that 'can be leveraged without authentication and leads to executing arbitrary code.' This is the primary initial access vector and should trigger alerts on unusual HTTP requests to DD-WRT management interfaces.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DD-WRT router management endpoints for requests with malformed buffer overflow payloads or high-entropy POST data. Look for HTTP 400/500 responses followed by suspicious process execution. Correlate failed HTTP requests with subsequent shell command execution or binary downloads.

suggestion.title: Detect SSH/Telnet Brute-Force from Compromised Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies the botnet 'downloads a Python script' that 'attempts to brute-force weak Telnet and SSH credentials' and 'uses worker threads to randomly scan internet-facing systems on common ports like 22 (SSH), 23 (Telnet).' This lateral movement vector should be detectable via failed login storms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on rapid SSH/Telnet login failures (>10 failures per minute per source IP) from non-admin networks. Correlate failed attempts with successful logins within 60 seconds. Cross-reference source IPs against known IoT device subnets and DD-WRT admin networks.

suggestion.title: Detect Malware Persistence via Cron Job Creation
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'creates cron jobs that relaunch it every 15 minutes' and the malware 'copies itself to hidden locations such as '/tmp/.sys', '/var/tmp/.sys', and '/dev/shm/.sys'.' Regular cron jobs for newly-placed binaries in /tmp are anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor crontab modification events and creation of cron entries. Alert on cron jobs referencing /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm directories, especially with intervals ≤15 minutes. Baseline legitimate system cron jobs and flag deviations.

suggestion.title: Detect Shell Startup Script Modification for Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'shell startup files are modified to enable automatic execution.' Modifications to .bashrc, .bash_profile, .profile, or similar files should be monitored for suspicious code injections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on writes to shell initialization files in /home, /root, or other user directories. Flag modifications that append commands, set environment variables pointing to /tmp, or invoke binaries from unusual locations. Baseline legitimate administrative changes.

suggestion.title: Detect Process Termination of Competing Malware and Security Tools
suggestion.rationale: Article details C0XMO 'actively scans running processes to identify competitor botnet clients... red-team tools, programming tools, and network services that may interfere with its operation, and terminates them. It does so by deleting binaries and removing their persistence mechanisms.' Mass process kills or selective tool termination is anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for rapid process termination events, especially of known security tools, remote-access tools, or competing malware (Mirai, Qbot, etc.). Alert on process kill followed by file deletion of the same binary. Flag patterns where the terminating process is non-standard (e.g., shell script, Python interpreter).

suggestion.title: Detect Network Scanning on High-Risk Port Set
suggestion.rationale: Article states the Python scanner 'scans internet-facing systems on common ports like 22 (SSH), 23 (Telnet), 80/443 (HTTP/HTTPS), 7547, 8080, 8443, 8888, and others.' This distinctive port combination (Telnet + HTTP variants + 7547 UPnP) is characteristic of IoT botnet reconnaissance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on systematic connection attempts from a single source to the port set {22, 23, 80, 443, 7547, 8080, 8443, 8888} across multiple targets in short time windows. Correlate with failed SSH/Telnet logins. Flag if source is a previously-compromised IoT device (residential IP, router, NVR).

suggestion.title: Cgroups v1 release_agent Modification by Unprivileged Process
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states vulnerability 'affects Linux systems using the cgroups v1 release_agent feature' and is 'actively leveraged in real-world attacks.' Modification of release_agent is the exploitation vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for writes to /sys/fs/cgroup/*/release_agent or /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern originating from unprivileged processes (UID > 0). Flag sequences where cgroup file modification precedes privilege elevation or command execution.

suggestion.title: Unprivileged Process Elevation via Cgroup Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article describes CVE-2022-0492 'may allow attackers' to escalate—attack pattern involves unprivileged user gaining elevated execution context through cgroup features.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when unprivileged process (UID > 0) spawns child with elevated EUID or capabilities, especially when preceded by cgroup syscalls (cgroup2_mkdir, open/write to cgroup control files) or release_agent path modifications.

suggestion.title: Kernel Privilege Escalation Exploitation Signature — CVE-2022-0492
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes active real-world exploitation; behavioral signatures must supplement asset exposure. Kernel-level cgroup interaction pattern is the tactical indicator of the attack.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect abnormal kernel interaction sequences: rapid cgroup control file creation/writes by unprivileged user, cgroup2_mkdir syscalls, then openat/write to /sys/fs/cgroup/*/release_agent, followed by process execution with privilege transition. Correlate timing between file modification and elevated process spawn.

suggestion.title: Credential Exposure – High-Profile Account PII Leakage Post-Disclosure
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states flaw 'exposed unredacted email addresses and phone numbers' for accounts including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Exposed contact info creates immediate phishing and account-takeover surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for bulk email/phone pairings from Instagram user accounts appearing in credential paste sites, dark web markets, and OSINT leaks within 48 hours post-disclosure (June 6–7). Cross-reference exposed addresses with corporate directories of high-profile targets.

suggestion.title: Phishing Campaigns – Spearphishing High-Profile Users with Exposed Contact Info
suggestion.rationale: Disclosed user emails and phone numbers (Mark Zuckerberg, Georgina Rodriguez named) are prime targets for follow-on phishing/smishing. Article confirms access to sensitive contact metadata.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for phishing emails impersonating Instagram/Meta targeting disclosed email addresses. Watch for SMS phishing to exposed phone numbers. Flag newly registered domains/phishing infrastructure created June 6–7 with keyword patterns targeting 'Instagram reset' or 'account verification.'

suggestion.title: Account Takeover via Credential Stuffing – Exposed Contact Details Enable Reset Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Exposed email/phone pairs directly enable password-reset abuse and account takeover. No authentication bypass needed if attacker possesses valid account email/phone.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect spike in failed Instagram login attempts using known-exposed email/phone combinations. Flag successful authentications from new geolocations or devices for disclosed high-profile accounts within 24–72 hours post-disclosure. Monitor for password-reset request anomalies.

suggestion.title: Callback Phishing + Remote Support Tool Installation
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers send 'invoice-themed phishing emails from consumer email accounts' containing 'no malicious links or attachments' and instead serve as 'precursor for follow-up phone calls' leading to 'remote support sessions' and installation of 'AnyDesk, Zoho Assist, Bomgar, or SuperOps'. Clear execution chain warranting detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for consumer email account senders (domains outside corporate whitelist) followed within 12 hours by network connections to known RMM tool C2 servers (AnyDesk, Zoho Assist, Bomgar, SuperOps). Correlate phishing recipients with subsequent RMM binary execution.

suggestion.title: Phishing Domain Pattern: Impersonated IT Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies attackers register domains following patterns '<organization>-itdesk[.]com', '<organization>-it[.]com', '<organization>-helpdesk[.]com' to impersonate internal IT portals. These are structural IoCs indicating preparatory reconnaissance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS queries and URL visits to domains matching pattern '*-itdesk.com', '*-it.com', '*-helpdesk.com' from external sources. Alert on SSL certificate registrations for these patterns within 5 days of known Silent Ransom targets.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration via WinSCP and Rclone
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'attackers commonly target document management platforms and cloud storage repositories before exfiltrating the data using tools such as WinSCP or Rclone'. Clear exfiltration vector with named tools.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process execution of winscp.exe, rclone.exe, or related binaries on systems without prior patch/deployment records. Alert on establishment of SFTP/SCP connections from office networks to external cloud storage providers. Track bulk document downloads from SharePoint/Teams preceding exfil tool execution.

suggestion.title: Privnote Self-Destructing Message Service Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article states threat actors 'use privnote[.]com, a self-destructing messaging service, to share installation links and commands with targets during remote support sessions' specifically 'to reduce forensic artifacts'. Named infrastructure used for C2 obfuscation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block or alert on all traffic to privnote[.]com from office networks. Monitor email bodies and Teams messages for privnote.com links. Flag employees receiving privnote links during hours matching remote support session timeframes (outside business hours).

suggestion.title: Fast-Flux Leak Site Domain Access
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'business-data-leaks[.]com' leak site and notes attackers use 'residential proxy networks spread across Latin America, Eastern Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Asia' to hide infrastructure. Named leak domain requires blocking/monitoring.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain blocklist for business-data-leaks[.]com and related Resecurity-identified infrastructure. Monitor DNS resolution patterns for rapid IP address changes indicative of fast-flux. Alert if any internal user accesses known Silent Ransom leak domains.

suggestion.title: Bulk Sensitive Document Access from Remote Support Sessions
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attackers who 'search for sensitive legal and financial documents, including contracts, tax records, Social Security numbers, and merger or acquisition files' from 'document management platforms and cloud storage repositories' following remote support session establishment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for abnormal bulk access patterns to SharePoint document libraries, Teams file storage, or OneDrive occurring within 30 minutes of RMM tool installation or Quick Assist/Terminal Services session. Alert on access to folders tagged as containing M&A plans, tax documents, or SSN data by accounts with no prior access history.

suggestion.title: FFmpeg Process Crash or Memory Corruption via Malicious File Input
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions '21 Zero-Days in FFmpeg'—these are almost certainly exploited via crafted media files passed to the ffmpeg binary. Pipeline should detect abnormal termination or crash patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for ffmpeg.exe processes spawned with file arguments pointing to unusual or recently-created media files, followed by access violations or segmentation faults. Alert on ffmpeg crash loops or execution timeouts within seconds of launch.

suggestion.title: Chrome Renderer Process Crash or Privilege Escalation Post-Patch
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Chrome Patches Record 429 Bugs'—likely includes memory safety issues (use-after-free, buffer overflow). Detection should capture exploitation attempts before patches are deployed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for chrome.exe or chromium processes with abnormal child processes spawned (cmd.exe, powershell.exe) immediately following a renderer process crash. Also monitor for unexpected elevation attempts from chrome's sandboxed renderer context.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Delivery via Compromised or Malicious Media Server
suggestion.rationale: Zero-day exploit delivery mechanisms for FFmpeg would typically involve hosting malicious media files on attacker infrastructure. Article mentions AI agent 'uncovered' vulnerabilities, implying active exploitation research.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect downloads of media files (.mkv, .mp4, .flv, .mov) from suspicious or newly-registered domains, followed by immediate ffmpeg processing. Correlate with process crashes or high CPU/memory spikes in ffmpeg child processes.

suggestion.title: Automated Vulnerability Research Tool Execution and Data Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly attributes discovery to 'AI Agent'—this suggests automated fuzzing, symbolic execution, or corpus-based testing framework activity. Should detect such tools and their output staging.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for execution of fuzzing frameworks (libFuzzer, AFL, honggfuzz), symbolic execution engines (KLEE, Triton), or security research tools (IDA, Ghidra, radare2) spawning abnormally high numbers of child processes or file I/O operations. Alert on bulk exfiltration of crash dumps or proof-of-concept payloads.

suggestion.title: CVE or Vulnerability ID Intelligence Gap
suggestion.rationale: Article references '21 Zero-Days' and '429 Bugs' by count, not CVE identifier. Pipeline should have either flagged missing CVE data or generated generic vulnerability monitoring rules pending CVE publication.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create provisional use-case rules for 'unpatched FFmpeg version X.Y execution on user endpoint' and 'unpatched Chrome version X execution', pending release of official CVE numbers. Use file version signatures or process memory signatures to identify vulnerable binaries in real-time.

suggestion.title: SolarWinds Serv-U Service Crash or Unexpected Restart
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly identifies 'DoS Flaw'—denial-of-service inherently manifests as process termination, hang, or restart cycles. No impact-phase detection was generated despite this being the primary attack observable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Serv-U process (srvagent.exe, FileAgent.exe) for unplanned termination or rapid restart cycles outside maintenance windows. Baseline expected uptime per environment and alert when restarts exceed threshold (e.g., >3 restarts per 10 minutes).

suggestion.title: Anomalous Network Traffic to Serv-U Service Ports
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability is 'actively exploited'—exploitation requires network delivery mechanism. No network-layer indicators or traffic anomaly detections generated despite this being observable at packet level.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on inbound traffic spikes or malformed packets to Serv-U listening ports (typically FTP 21, SSH 22). Flag traffic from multiple sources with high request velocity or packet patterns consistent with DoS payloads.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable SolarWinds Serv-U Version Inventory
suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV catalog entries are version-specific. Article title implies a known, documented vulnerability affecting specific Serv-U builds, but no asset inventory or version-matching IOCs were extracted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Asset query: identify Serv-U installations with version strings matching CISA KEV affected-version ranges. Cross-reference against SolarWinds patch advisories and alert on unpatched instances in production.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-20245 Exploitation Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states the CVE is 'actively exploited'; this is the core IOC the pipeline missed entirely. Any Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager deployment becomes a detection target.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP requests to Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager admin interfaces with patterns consistent with CVE-2026-20245 exploitation (malformed parameters, known payload signatures, or unexpected API calls from non-authenticated sources). Correlate with administrative access logs to identify successful compromise.

suggestion.title: Cisco SD-WAN Manager Reconnaissance and Fingerprinting
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'active exploitation' implying attacker reconnaissance phase; no UC generated for probing or enumeration of vulnerable systems prior to exploitation attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect scanning behavior targeting SD-WAN Manager ports and endpoints: version detection probes, admin panel requests to non-existent paths, or repeated failed authentication attempts consistent with fingerprinting.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement from Compromised SD-WAN Manager
suggestion.rationale: Successful exploitation of a management plane device (SD-WAN Manager) would pivot into internal networks; pipeline did not suggest lateral movement detection despite 'no patch available' language implying persistent compromise risk.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for internal network connections, file transfers, and command execution originating from the SD-WAN Manager host post-compromise, particularly to non-adjacent network segments or high-value targets.

suggestion.title: Everest Forms Pro PHP eval() Code Injection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'sanitize_text_field() function, which does not escape single quotes (\') or other characters that influence PHP syntax' allowing 'close the intended string, inject arbitrary PHP code.' This is the core vulnerability mechanism and requires detection of malformed form submissions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Everest Forms calculation form submissions for quote characters, PHP syntax tokens (=, $, ;, //, #), or payloads containing wp_insert_user(). Alert on POST requests to form endpoints containing semicolons or comment markers followed by PHP keywords.

suggestion.title: WordPress Admin Account Creation via Form Processing
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'call wp_insert_user() to create a new administrator account.' Legitimate admin creation occurs through WordPress admin UI, not form calculation logic. Direct detection opportunity for persistence mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect wp_insert_user() function calls originating from form processing code (wp-content/plugins/everest-forms-pro/). Alert on new user creation with administrator role immediately following form submission, especially with suspicious usernames.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Admin User Creation with Indicator Username
suggestion.rationale: Article notes defenders should 'review log files and administrator accounts for any suspicious activity, especially containing the string diksimarina.' This is the concrete IOC for persistence; admin creation attempts without legitimate UI interaction are anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search WordPress user tables and audit logs for account creation events where username contains 'diksimarina' or matches pattern of random character sequences not matching organizational naming conventions. Flag any admin role assignments tied to form processing timestamps.

suggestion.title: Form Field Injection with Comment Escape Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article specifically describes 'trailing // comment marker ensures the rest of the generated PHP code...is treated as a comment.' Form fields containing comment syntax (// or #) are non-standard and indicate injection attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on form submissions where field values contain comment markers (//, #, /* */) or single quotes immediately followed by PHP operators ($, =, ;). These indicate attempt to break out of string context and inject code.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Traffic from Known Attacker IPs
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'exploitation attempts originate primarily from two IP addresses, 202.56.2[.]126 and 209.146.60.26' and that Wordfence blocked over 29,300 attempts. These are documented active attacker IPs with high confidence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block or alert on traffic from 202.56.2.126 and 209.146.60.26 reaching WordPress sites running Everest Forms Pro <= 1.9.12. Correlate with form submission attempts and check for successful admin account creation within timeframe.

suggestion.title: Suspicious App Installation on Smart TV Device
suggestion.rationale: Article premise: free apps installed by users on smart TVs are 'quietly turning' them into proxies. Requires detection of third-party app installs outside official channels—cite 'Free Apps Are Quietly Turning Smart TVs'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor smart TV / streaming device app store installation logs for apps from unknown publishers or installation via sideloading. Detect package installation outside official OS app stores; correlate with user reports of unexpected app appearance.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Web Scraping Traffic from Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Core attack: apps 'scraping' web content. Must detect repeated HTTP/HTTPS GET requests to non-entertainment URLs, high-volume content fetching inconsistent with normal viewing—cite 'Web-Scraping Proxies'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect smart TV devices initiating large volumes of HTTP requests to diverse domains unrelated to streaming/media (e.g., news sites, e-commerce, SaaS platforms). Flag patterns indicating systematic content harvesting: high request frequency, robots.txt parsing, sequential URL enumeration.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration from Smart TV to External C2
suggestion.rationale: Apps act as proxies: scraped data must be sent somewhere. Article states content is sent to attackers for AI training—requires egress detection—cite 'proxies for AI'.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify outbound connections from smart TV to non-trusted IP ranges, especially to cloud storage or C2 infrastructure. Flag devices exfiltrating compressed/archived data, large-volume uploads to unrecognized endpoints, or encrypted payloads to unknown destinations.

suggestion.title: Persistence of Malicious Smart TV App Across Reboot
suggestion.rationale: Apps must survive reboots to act as long-lived proxies. Article implies ongoing background activity—cite 'Quietly Turning' (implies continuous operation).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor smart TV app persistence mechanisms: auto-start registry/config entries, startup folders, scheduled tasks, or background service registration. Correlate app installation events with boot logs to confirm apps re-launch post-reboot.

suggestion.title: Smart TV Network Lateral Movement to Other Home Devices
suggestion.rationale: Compromised smart TV may pivot to other IoT or home network devices. Article focuses on TV but doesn't explicitly rule out spread—gap in coverage for multi-device infection chains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect smart TV scanning home network ranges, probing other devices on same subnet, or attempting unauthorized access to routers, NAS, or other connected devices. Flag SMB/SSH brute-force attempts originating from smart TV.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated or Encrypted Payload Execution on Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Malicious apps likely use code obfuscation or encryption to evade detection. Article does not specify how apps hide behavior—detection gap for anti-analysis techniques.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual process spawning (shell interpreters, dynamic loaders) launched by app processes. Detect memory-only code injection, runtime decryption of payloads, or base64/hex encoding in app strings. Flag debugger or emulation-detection calls.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Smart TV App Installing Proxy Components
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Free apps available on Samsung, LG, Roku… have been quietly enrolling millions of living room devices into a commercial residential proxy network.' Pipeline missed initial-access detection. Need to hunt for app installations pulling proxy client SDKs or connecting to bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com early in lifecycle.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Smart TV apps spawning child processes or loading libraries matching bright-sdk, brdtnet, or luminati patterns. Monitor app-store installations on Samsung/LG devices for suspicious permissions requests (network access, persistence, data exfiltration).

suggestion.title: Smart TV Outbound Traffic to Residential Proxy Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'enrolling devices into a… residential proxy network… used to scrape web data.' Pipeline extracted IOCs but generated no network detection use case. Detection must pair IP/domain IOCs (3.33.193.183, 15.197.193.114, proxyjs.brdtnet.com, etc.) with TV device telemetry.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Living-room devices (Samsung/LG smart TVs, Roku) initiating connections to bright-sdk.com, proxyjs.luminatinet.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com, or known proxy-service IPs. Baseline: these IPs/domains should have zero legitimate TV traffic. Correlation with app installation 0-24h prior.

suggestion.title: Unexpected HTTP Traffic Patterns Consistent with Web Scraping from Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'scrape web data for AI training.' The exfiltration phase (collection → C2 → external) is not represented in any use case. Need behavioral detection for TV devices issuing high-volume GET requests or sustained HTTP sessions unusual for a living-room appliance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Smart TV devices generating sustained or spiking HTTP traffic (>1000 requests/hour, 100+ unique domains per hour) inconsistent with normal TV usage (video streaming, app store, UI). Detect proxy-header patterns (X-Forwarded-For, Via) or User-Agent strings indicating proxy client SDK.

suggestion.title: Deceptive Consent Burial in Smart TV App Navigation
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'consent dialog buried in a TV remote's arrow-key navigation.' This defense-evasion tactic (hiding proxy opt-in in dense UI) is a behavioral indicator. No use case captured this social-engineering vector or the app's attempt to obscure permissions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Analyze smart TV app manifests and runtime behavior for permission dialogs that require non-standard navigation (e.g., multiple arrow-key presses, buried in sub-menus, text truncated). Cross-reference with domains/IOCs from proxy infrastructure.

suggestion.title: BrightData/Luminati Residential Proxy Service Abuse via Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Article IOCs (brdtnet.com, luminatinet.com, bright-sdk.com, luminati.io) are confirmed infrastructure of BrightData, a legitimate proxy service. Detection must differentiate abuse (malicious app enrollment) from legitimate BrightData customer usage. No use case addresses this contextual IOC interpretation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Connections to bright-sdk.com, luminatinet.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com FROM smart TV devices (non-corporate, non-VPN contexts) are high-confidence abuse indicators. Correlate with app installation of unknown publishers. Legitimate enterprise BrightData usage is from corporate networks and dedicated appliances, not consumer TVs.

suggestion.title: Supply-Chain Compromise: Malicious App Distribution via Smart TV App Stores
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Free apps… have been quietly enrolling… devices… according to new research from Include Security.' Pipeline did not map the app-store supply-chain attack vector. Need detection for apps appearing in Samsung/LG/Roku stores that match malicious signature or behavioral profile post-installation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Samsung SmartThings, LG Content Store, Roku Channel Store for apps with zero legitimate reviews, suspicious publishers, or post-installation behavior matching proxy-client patterns (network socket creation, library loading for bright-sdk, persistence hooks).

suggestion.title: Supply-Chain Malware Delivery via Repository Commit
suggestion.rationale: Title: 'Miasma Worm Hits 73 Microsoft GitHub Repositories' — attack vector is code repository compromise. Malware injected into repos will execute on downstream consumers' build pipelines and development environments.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect commits containing known malware signatures, suspicious binary/executable payloads, or obfuscated scripting code in version-controlled repositories. Alert on staged payload commits: scripts that download/exec secondary malware. Prioritize high-value repos (Microsoft core libraries, infrastructure code).

suggestion.title: Bulk Repository Modification Across Organizational Portfolio
suggestion.rationale: 73 simultaneous repo compromises suggests coordinated, account-driven attack. Should detect anomalous single-actor mass modifications across multiple critical repositories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag single account/service principal modifying >20 repositories within 60-minute window. Baseline per-account repo-write rates; alert on deviations. Monitor for disabling branch protections, removing required reviewers, or force-pushing to protected branches in bulk.

suggestion.title: Worm Self-Propagation via Code Repository
suggestion.rationale: Article names malware 'Worm' implying self-propagating capability. Should detect code patterns enabling cross-repo replication or staged infection chains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify commits with recursive/automated repo-cloning logic, commit loops, or parameterized scripts that iterate across multiple targets. Detect build scripts launching external executables or downloading payloads from attacker-controlled domains during CI/CD execution.

suggestion.title: Compromised Dependency Manifest Injection
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attack lasting across 73 repos will propagate via package dependencies (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml, etc.). Downstream builds will fetch infected versions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor changes to dependency manifests for unexpected version pins, new malicious dependencies, or URLs pointing to attacker infrastructure. Detect commits adding post-install scripts or build hooks that execute arbitrary code. Alert on version-bump patterns that deviate from team norm.

suggestion.title: Defense Evasion via Repository Policy Disablement
suggestion.rationale: Successful compromise of 73 repos requires bypassing/disabling security controls (branch protections, code review requirements, signed commits). Should detect policy removals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on API calls disabling branch protection rules, removing required code reviewers, disabling signed-commit requirements, or removing repository collaborators on high-value projects. Correlate with subsequent suspicious commit/push activity from previously-restricted accounts.

suggestion.title: Malware Execution via CI/CD Pipeline Hijacking
suggestion.rationale: Injected worm code will execute when repositories are built/deployed. Build agents (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins) become execution vectors for malware.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor build job execution for unexpected process spawning (cmd.exe, powershell, curl, wget) during build/test phases. Detect outbound network connections from build agents to non-whitelisted domains, or lateral movement attempts from build infrastructure to internal networks. Baseline normal build process execution trees.

suggestion.title: Suspicious GitHub Actions Repository Modifications
suggestion.rationale: Article describes compromise of 'Azure Functions Action' and 72 other repositories via supply-chain attack ('Azure Functions Action and 72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack')—pipeline missed detection of unauthorized action definitions or workflow file modifications in version-control audit logs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for creation or modification of .github/workflows/*.yml files or action.yml in high-trust repositories; alert on unsigned commits, commits by new accounts, or changes to action metadata (run steps, permissions, secrets access). Establish baseline of legitimate maintainers.

suggestion.title: Mass Automated Disabling of Repositories
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states '72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack'—suggests coordinated, high-volume destructive actions post-compromise. Pipeline should have flagged batch disabling as impact indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on bulk repository deletion, archival, or access-control changes within short time window (e.g., >5 repos in <1 hour). Correlate with non-routine account activity, unusual API token usage, or out-of-hours administrative actions. Baseline per organization.

suggestion.title: Malicious Artifact in AI Coding Agent Tools
suggestion.rationale: Article targets 'AI Coding Agents'—pipeline did not identify specific detection for compromise of tooling used in LLM-augmented development pipelines (GitHub Copilot, Codex integrations, etc.). Suggests backdoored packages or poisoned code suggestions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected package versions, checksum mismatches, or dependency updates in AI agent tool stacks. Flag installation of packages with suspicious names similar to legitimate tools. Cross-reference with public advisories on poisoned dependencies.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Azure Functions Deployment via Compromised Action
suggestion.rationale: Title specifies 'Azure Functions Action'—compromised GitHub Action allowed malicious deployments to Azure. Pipeline missed detection of malicious function definitions or unexpected Azure deployments from CI/CD pipelines.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate GitHub Actions execution (especially from modified azure-functions-action) with Azure Functions deployment events. Alert on deployments with suspicious code patterns, unexpected resource access, or exfiltration attempts in function code.

suggestion.title: Abnormal CI/CD Pipeline Secret Access Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attacks via compromised actions typically exfiltrate secrets (API keys, deploy tokens). Article does not detail exfil mechanism but pipeline should flag access to repository secrets during suspicious action runs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for enumeration or access of GitHub Secrets, Azure Key Vault, or environment variables within action runs. Flag reference to secrets in logs, unexpected curl/wget to external endpoints, or secrets passed to unrecognized tools.

suggestion.title: Reuse of Miasma Malware Infrastructure in Supply Chain Context
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'Miasma Worm Hits Microsoft Again'—suggests known threat actor repeating TTP. Pipeline should flag if Miasma C2 domains, certificates, or repository registrations appear in scanning data or whois records.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference IOCs from prior Miasma incidents (if public) with newly registered domains, certificates, or hosting. Flag GitHub organization registrations with patterns matching prior actor infrastructure. Correlate with action repository metadata (owner, contact emails).

suggestion.title: Suspicious PyPI Package Installation – durabletask
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'Microsoft's durabletask PyPI Package Compromised'; pipeline must detect installation of affected package versions from package repositories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on pip install, poetry add, or similar commands for durabletask package. Flag version numbers outside documented release schedule or from unsigned/unverified sources. Correlate installation with downstream suspicious execution.

suggestion.title: Malicious Code Execution from Python Package Initialization
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks execute payload at import time. The article describes a compromised package; detection must trigger on unexpected child processes or network calls spawned during module load.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Python process spawning curl, wget, powershell, or sh during durabletask import or initialization. Suspicious network egress from python.exe to non-CDN IPs immediately post-installation. Monitor subprocess.Popen or os.system calls within site-packages/durabletask.

suggestion.title: Credential or Environment Variable Exfiltration from Python
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks commonly harvest .env files, API keys, and AWS credentials. Article describes a 'supply chain attack' without specifying payload—exfiltration is a standard goal.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Python process reading .env, .aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/config, requirements.txt, or pip.conf outside normal developer workflow. HTTP POST from Python with Base64/gzip payloads to suspicious domains. File access patterns suggesting credential enumeration.

suggestion.title: PyPI Package Tampering – Hash Verification Mismatch
suggestion.rationale: Compromised package would have different file hashes than official release. Pipeline should detect when installed durabletask files fail validation against PyPI manifest.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hash mismatch between installed site-packages/durabletask/*.py files and official PyPI checksums. Metadata tampering detected via wheel/egg signature validation. Anomalous file timestamps (e.g., .pyc modified outside source modification window).

suggestion.title: Suspicious Version Download or Repository Proxy Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article describes supply chain attack on PyPI; detection must cover unusual package repository queries, version enumeration, or downloads from mirrors/proxies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Rapid sequential downloads of durabletask versions from PyPI or mirrors. Requests to index.pypi.org with unusual user-agents or from suspicious IP ranges. Pip operations with --index-url pointing to attacker-controlled or non-standard registries.

suggestion.title: CVE-2021-27137 DD-WRT Buffer Overflow Exploitation Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names CVE-2021-27137 as the exploitation vector used for initial delivery: 'exploiting CVE-2021-27137, a buffer overflow vulnerability caused by insufficient user input.' This is the root attack surface and should trigger on unauthenticated requests with oversized payloads to DD-WRT endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unauthenticated HTTP requests to DD-WRT admin interfaces (/apply.cgi, /admin paths) with abnormally large Content-Length headers or buffer-overflow-like payloads. Flag POST requests with parameter values exceeding typical sizes for router settings.

suggestion.title: Cron Job Registration for 15-Minute Re-execution
suggestion.rationale: Article states explicitly: 'creates cron jobs that relaunch it every 15 minutes.' This is deterministic persistence behavior and should fire on any crontab entry with */15 minute intervals pointing to suspicious paths.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect new cron job entries with */15 minute scheduling. Correlate with suspicious binary locations (/tmp/.sys, /var/tmp/.sys, /dev/shm/.sys) or with processes spawned from hidden temporary directories. Alert on crontab write operations from non-standard processes.

suggestion.title: ELF Binary Placement in Hidden Temp Directories
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies persistence locations: 'copies itself to hidden locations such as /tmp/.sys, /var/tmp/.sys, and /dev/shm/.sys.' This pattern is high-confidence indicator of malicious activity and should trigger file integrity monitoring.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect file writes to .sys hidden directories in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm with ELF magic bytes. Flag multi-architecture binaries (ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, x86, x86_64) being dropped in the same session, indicating architecture-aware deployment.

suggestion.title: Multi-threaded SSH/Telnet Credential Brute-Force from Python Scanner
suggestion.rationale: Article details the scanning phase: 'uses worker threads to randomly scan internet-facing systems on common ports like 22 (SSH), 23 (Telnet)... attempts to brute-force weak Telnet and SSH credentials.' This is detectable as rapid distributed authentication failures.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect >10 failed SSH/Telnet login attempts from single source to multiple destinations within 5-minute window. Correlate with python process execution. Flag 'paramiko' library imports and concurrent worker processes suggesting multi-threaded attack.

suggestion.title: Python Scanning Package Installation (paramiko, requests, beautifulsoup4)
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'downloads a Python script that installs additional packages such as requests, paramiko, and beautifulsoup4.' Concurrent installation of these three packages is rare in production and strongly indicative of scanning framework setup.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect pip or python subprocess execution installing paramiko+requests+beautifulsoup4 bundle in rapid sequence. High-confidence alert if source is binary in /tmp or /var/tmp. Flag any non-standard user or service account context.

suggestion.title: Competing Botnet and Red-Team Tool Termination Sequence
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes: 'actively scans running processes to identify competitor botnet clients on the host... and terminates them... by deleting binaries and removing their persistence mechanisms, including cron jobs, init scripts, system services, and shell profile entries.' This defensive batch-kill pattern is detectable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect sequence of rapid process terminations (pkill, kill commands) followed by file deletions from /etc/cron.d, /etc/init.d, or shell profiles. Flag termination of known botnet client names (mirai, qbot, tsunami variants) or security tool names in batch.

suggestion.title: cgroup v1 release_agent Modification Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article specifically mentions 'cgroups v1 release_agent feature' as the exploitation vector. Pipeline generated zero use cases around this known attack primitive. Release_agent write attempts directly establish exploitation intent.
log_sources: Auditd logs (access to /proc/*/cgroup, write to cgroup.release_agent)
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for writes to cgroup.release_agent file or path traversal patterns targeting /proc/[pid]/cgroup on Linux systems. Correlate with processes holding CAP_SYS_ADMIN or running in non-root namespaces. CVE-2022-0492 exploitation requires direct write to release_agent file; legitimate usage is rare.

suggestion.title: Privilege Escalation Following cgroup Namespace Manipulation
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies this as improper authentication leading to attacker capability. Privilege escalation is the implicit impact, yet no detection covers UID/GID elevation post-cgroup write. Pipeline missed explicit privilege escalation phase entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline of cgroup-related file access patterns (writes to cgroup namespace files). Trigger on subsequent privilege escalation (UID change from non-root to root, or capability acquisition) within 5 minutes. Elevated confidence if source process lacks CAP_SYS_ADMIN prior to cgroup manipulation.

suggestion.title: Arbitrary Command Execution via cgroup.release_agent
suggestion.rationale: Cgroups v1 release_agent is a command execution mechanism — when a cgroup is destroyed, the release_agent executable is invoked. Article doesn't detail specific command payloads, but exploitation inherently involves command execution. No detection for suspicious release_agent invocation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process execution patterns consistent with cgroup release_agent callbacks: short-lived child processes spawned after cgroup.release_agent write, especially shell interpreters or unusual binaries executed from /proc or /tmp. Correlate with prior cgroup file access.

suggestion.title: Container Escape via cgroups v1 (Containerized Environments)
suggestion.rationale: CVE-2022-0492 is commonly exploited for container escape. Article context mentions Linux systems broadly; containerized deployments are high-value targets. Pipeline generated no environment-specific detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: In Kubernetes/container environments, detect processes escaping pod namespace constraints after cgroup manipulation: host mount access from container, /host filesystem access, or host PID/network namespace joins. Baseline normal cgroup operations per workload and alert on anomalies.

suggestion.title: Defensive evasion: Manipulation of cgroup Security Controls
suggestion.rationale: Article categorizes flaw as 'improper authentication' — implies a security control is bypassed. No defense-evasion use case generated despite this being core to the threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for disabled or circumvented security controls (AppArmor, SELinux) preceding cgroup manipulation. Detect cgroup operations that bypass resource limits or access controls. Alert on suppressed audit logging following cgroup writes (potential cover-track attempt).

suggestion.title: Password Reset Endpoint Abuse Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'critical logic bug in Instagram's web-based password reset flow' but pipeline generated zero detection use cases for auth endpoint anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor password reset endpoints for: rapid sequential reset requests on same account, successful resets without preceding login, or resets followed by account access from anomalous IP/device/geography within 1 hour. Establish baseline velocity per user and per source IP.

suggestion.title: Bulk User Enumeration via Password Reset
suggestion.rationale: Article describes exposure of 'unredacted email addresses and phone numbers associated with user accounts' — attackers can enumerate users systematically. No enumeration detection suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on high-volume password reset initiation requests (>100 unique targets/hour) from single IP or session. Flag requests using leaked credential lists or sequential username/email patterns. Monitor for differential error responses that leak user existence.

suggestion.title: Post-Reset Account Takeover of High-Profile Accounts
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly notes impact on 'high-profile individuals such as Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and model Georgina Rodriguez' but no secondary exploitation detection for sensitive accounts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate successful password resets on VIP/executive accounts with subsequent logins from geographic distance >1000km or new device within 1 hour. Flag as priority if email/phone exposed during vulnerability window matches public records of targeted individuals.

suggestion.title: Unredacted PII in API Response Logging
suggestion.rationale: The vulnerability exposed unredacted contact fields — detection should identify when password reset/account recovery endpoints return full email or phone number instead of masked format.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parse password reset and account recovery API responses for unredacted PII fields (full phone/email vs last-4-digits format). Alert on bulk access to these endpoints returning unmasked contact data, especially from automated or high-velocity sources.

suggestion.title: Callback Phishing Detection - Invoice Email Trigger
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'attacks begin with invoice-themed phishing emails from consumer email accounts. These emails do not contain malicious links or attachments and instead serve as a precursor for follow-up phone calls from attackers impersonating corporate IT staff.' No detection generated for this multi-stage initial access pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails with invoice-related subject/body lures sent from free email providers to law firm employee distribution lists, followed within 4 hours by inbound calls, Teams meeting invitations, or Zoom URLs from the email sender's phone number or domain. Flag sender WHOIS registrant mismatch with company name.

suggestion.title: Remote Access Tool Installation Following Phishing Callback
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'threat actors trick the target into installing remote monitoring and management tools such as AnyDesk, Zoho Assist, Bomgar, or SuperOps' during remote support sessions. These five tools are primary attack vector and warrant behavioral detection post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on installation/execution of AnyDesk, Zoho Assist, Bomgar, or SuperOps (by process name, publisher, or unsigned installer hash) within 90 minutes of Teams/Zoom/Quick Assist session. Flag downloads from non-vendor domains, obfuscated executables, or execution from user AppData folders.

suggestion.title: Bulk Legal Document Access Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'Once inside a network, the group searches for sensitive legal and financial documents, including contracts, tax records, Social Security numbers, and merger or acquisition files' and 'commonly target document management platforms and cloud storage repositories.' No detection for pattern of rapid discovery/enumeration of sensitive repositories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid sequential file enumeration or access to SharePoint/OneDrive folders containing contracts, tax filings, or M&A documentation from user account with active RMM process. Look for >50 files accessed in <10 minutes from document repositories not previously accessed by that user.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration via WinSCP or Rclone
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names: 'The attackers commonly target document management platforms and cloud storage repositories before exfiltrating the data using tools such as WinSCP or Rclone.' These tools are legitimate but anomalous in law firm networks and warrant execution-based alerting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of winscp.exe or rclone.exe with network connections to external cloud storage (AWS S3, B2, Dropbox) or FTP endpoints. Correlate with recent RMM tool installation and bulk file access. Flag any usage from standard user profiles (non-IT), unsigned executables, or persistence mechanisms.

suggestion.title: Privnote[.]com Access During Remote Support Sessions
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'The researchers say the threat actors also use privnote[.]com, a self-destructing messaging service, to share installation links and commands with targets during remote support sessions...This tactic helps reduce forensic artifacts left in browser histories or corporate chat logs.' Legitimate service but contextually anomalous.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for access to privnote[.]com from law firm employee accounts during hours matching Teams/Zoom active sessions. Flag any privnote URLs containing base64-encoded content, shortened URLs, or links redirecting to AnyDesk/Zoho/Bomgar installation domains. Correlate with RMM process execution.

suggestion.title: Fast-Flux DNS Queries to Data-Leak Domains
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'Resecurity found that the gang is also operating fast-flux infrastructure' with 'business-data-leaks[.]com leak site and related infrastructure rely on residential proxy networks spread across Latin America, Eastern Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Asia.' No detection for internal access to attacker leak infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on DNS queries to business-data-leaks[.]com or pattern matches to fast-flux data-leak sites. Correlate resolution IPs against residential proxy databases (ISPdb, ABUSEIPDB). Flag single domain resolving to >15 different IPs in 24-hour window with subsequent connection attempts from law firm network.

suggestion.title: FFmpeg Vulnerable Version Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states '21 Zero-Days in FFmpeg'—pipeline must detect execution of known-vulnerable FFmpeg versions. Title alone establishes zero-day inventory but no version IOCs or detection rules were generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for FFmpeg process launch with command-line arguments that may trigger vulnerable codecs or input filters. Look for unusual parent processes spawning ffmpeg (web browsers, document handlers, media servers). Correlate against known vulnerable version hashes.

suggestion.title: Chrome Browser Exploitation via Patched Vulnerability
suggestion.rationale: Article cites 'Chrome Patches Record 429 Bugs'—implies active exploitation risk during transition window between vulnerability disclosure and patch adoption. No Chrome-specific detection rules generated despite HIGH severity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Chrome version mismatches between user agent and installed version (old user agents + recent timestamps suggest failed updates). Detect crash dumps or abnormal memory access patterns from chrome.exe or renderer processes. Alert on Chrome renderer sandbox escapes.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Payload Activity Following Zero-Day Disclosure
suggestion.rationale: Article scope implies potential active exploitation—'AI Agent Uncovers' suggests these are newly-discovered, not hypothetical. Pipeline failed to suggest heap-overflow, buffer-overflow, or memory-corruption detection signatures typical of FFmpeg/Chrome exploits.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for abnormal child process spawning from FFmpeg or Chrome (indicators of sandbox escape). Detect memory access violations, segmentation faults, or heap corruption signatures in process crash telemetry. Flag unexpected system calls or privilege escalation attempts from media processing threads.

suggestion.title: Unpatched Software Inventory Gap
suggestion.rationale: Article references 429 Chrome patches and 21 FFmpeg zero-days, implying rapid patching cycle. Pipeline should generate detection to identify systems lagging behind latest versions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query all FFmpeg and Chrome process launches; extract version from binary metadata, command-line args, or registry. Flag any instance running version older than publication date plus N days (grace period for patch testing). Correlate against CVSS scores to prioritize high-impact unpatched instances.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Service Crash or Abnormal Restart
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability causes 'DoS' and is 'actively exploited'—implies attacker-triggered service unavailability; pipeline missed detection for service termination/restart patterns that precede impact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Serv-U process exit codes and restart frequency within 5-minute windows. Baseline normal restarts during maintenance; flag sudden clusters of crashes or unexpected SIGTERM/SIGKILL signals correlated with external connection attempts.

suggestion.title: Malformed or Oversized Serv-U Protocol Request
suggestion.rationale: DoS flaws typically triggered by malformed or resource-exhaustion payloads; article does not detail exploitation mechanism but pipeline should have generated hypothesis for common DoS vectors.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Capture and profile legitimate Serv-U (SFTP/SSH or FTP) handshake sizes and request patterns. Alert on requests exceeding protocol-defined limits, rapid connection churn without auth completion, or byte sequences matching known CVE PoC signatures if disclosed.

suggestion.title: Serv-U Port Flooding or Rapid Connection Reset
suggestion.rationale: Application-layer DoS often manifests as connection exhaustion or reset storms; article's 'DoS' designation implies attacker can flood the service port.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline for TCP connections to Serv-U listening ports (default 22 for SSH, 21 for FTP, or proprietary port). Alert when connection-per-minute or concurrent connection count exceeds 3σ or when RST flag ratio jumps >50% within a 1-minute window.

suggestion.title: Spike in Serv-U Error or Diagnostic Logging
suggestion.rationale: DoS exploitation typically generates a burst of error or warning logs before service failure; pipeline did not suggest log-anomaly detection despite article emphasizing 'actively exploited' status.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Serv-U error/warning event count per minute. Baseline normal levels during business hours. Alert on >5× increase in ERROR or FATAL log lines within 2-minute interval, especially if preceded by spike in connection resets or timeouts.

suggestion.title: Cisco SD-WAN Manager Exploitation Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states CVE-2026-20245 is 'actively exploited' in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager with 'no patch available', but pipeline generated zero detection use cases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor SD-WAN Manager endpoints (typically TCP 8443, 8080) for exploitation signatures matching CVE-2026-20245 POC patterns. Flag HTTP requests with suspicious payloads, SQL injection, command injection, or path traversal attempts targeting known vulnerable URI paths in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager. Alert on authentication bypass patterns or direct admin panel access from unexpected network segments.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized SD-WAN Manager Access Post-Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Active exploitation creates post-compromise access patterns; article provides no visibility into defensive detection of credential use or lateral movement from compromised manager.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect anomalous administrative actions within Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager post-exploitation: bulk policy changes, device registration of unexpected gateways, traffic steering to external resolvers, encrypted tunnels to unknown endpoints, or configuration exports to untrusted destinations. Baseline normal policy update frequency and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: SD-WAN Manager Network Reconnaissance by Threat Actor
suggestion.rationale: If vulnerability allows command execution, reconnaissance activity should follow; pipeline did not map to discovery or lateral_movement phases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Cisco SD-WAN Manager logs for internal network scans, SNMP enumeration, device discovery queries, or WMI/SSH probes initiated from the manager process or authenticated sessions. Track DNS queries for internal infrastructure hostnames originating from the SD-WAN appliance network context.

suggestion.title: Cisco SD-WAN Manager Remote Code Execution Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title mentions active exploitation with no patch; RCE execution should be a high-confidence phase but pipeline produced zero execution-phase use cases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect process spawning from Cisco SD-WAN Manager services (e.g., tomcat, nginx, java process) with suspicious command lines: reverse shells, curl/wget to external IPs, PowerShell/bash with encoded arguments, or scripts written to /tmp. Monitor parent process relationships and user context (expect system/manager service account).

suggestion.title: Suspicious Admin Account Creation with Malicious Username
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'calls wp_insert_user() to create a new administrator account with the username diksimarina' and recommends defenders 'review log files and administrator accounts for any suspicious activity, especially containing the string diksimarina.' This is a concrete post-exploitation persistence indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on wp_insert_user() function execution within Everest Forms plugin context creating accounts with usernames matching known malicious patterns (e.g., 'diksimarina') or other suspicious admin-creation patterns. Correlate admin account creation timestamps with form submission logs during exploitation window (April 13, 2026 onward).

suggestion.title: PHP Code Injection via Form Field Quote-Prefix Attack
suggestion.rationale: Article describes exact attack: 'attacker submits a value for a text field that begins with a single quote to close the wrapping string literal, followed by a PHP statement' and uses 'trailing // comment marker.' This is signature injection pattern distinct to this vulnerability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP POST requests to Everest Forms form endpoints where field values begin with single quote (') or semicolon (;) immediately followed by PHP function calls (wp_, eval, system, exec, base64_decode) or end with '//' comment sequences. Flag payloads matching: '^[\'\"].*(?:wp_|eval|system|exec|shell_exec).*//'

suggestion.title: Requests from Known Everest Forms Exploitation IPs
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'exploitation attempts originate primarily from two IP addresses, 202.56.2.126 and 209.146.60.26' with 'firewall blocking over 29,300 attempts.' These are Wordfence-corroborated active exploitation sources requiring IP-based blocking.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block or alert on HTTP requests from source IPs 202.56.2.126 or 209.146.60.26 accessing any WordPress endpoint. These IPs are confirmed actively exploiting Everest Forms Pro CVE-2026-3300; any connection to vulnerable WordPress sites should be treated as compromise attempt.

suggestion.title: eval() Execution Within Everest Forms Complex Calculation Context
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies vulnerability mechanism: 'accepts values submitted through form fields and inserts them into a PHP code string. Then, it executes the resulting code using PHP's eval() function.' This is the core execution primitive requiring detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for eval() function invocations originating from Everest Forms plugin code paths (wp-content/plugins/everest-forms-pro/includes/*) with form-submission data as arguments. Alert on eval() receiving input containing unescaped single quotes or PHP keywords; this violates normal form calculation behavior.

suggestion.title: Plugin Version Vulnerability Match: Everest Forms Pro ≤1.9.12
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'security issue affects versions 1.9.12 and earlier of the plugin.' Defenders should identify installed plugin versions and flag outdated instances. Patch availability confirmed as March 18, 2026.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan WordPress installations for Everest Forms Pro plugin presence and version. Flag any instances running version 1.9.12 or earlier as vulnerable to CVE-2026-3300. Cross-reference against access logs from April 13, 2026 onward to determine exploitation timeline.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Outbound HTTP Requests from Smart TV Applications
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes apps 'quietly' perform web scraping for AI training—characteristic high-volume HTTP requests to external domains not associated with legitimate streaming/media services. Detect via unusual destination domains, request frequency, and volume patterns from TV device processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor smart TV devices for outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections originating from third-party app processes to high-entropy domain names or known content-serving platforms (news, shopping, social media) outside normal user browsing patterns. Baseline legitimate streaming traffic and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: Large-Scale Data Exfiltration from IoT Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article describes apps acting as 'proxies' for web scraping, implying significant bandwidth consumption and data exfiltration. This mirrors C2 tunnel behavior: detect via sustained high-volume outbound connections with minimal inbound response relative to data sent.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when a single smart TV device maintains persistent outbound connections with total bytes sent significantly exceeding bytes received (>10:1 ratio sustained over 5+ minutes), indicating one-way data exfiltration rather than request-response patterns typical of user-initiated media streaming.

suggestion.title: Unexpected Application Installation and Persistence on Smart TV
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates 'free apps' distributed to TVs without user knowledge or explicit consent, suggesting either sideloading, pre-installation, or deceptive app-store listings. Detect unusual app installation events outside normal user-initiated patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on app installation to smart TV devices via non-standard channels (sideload, silent update) or installation of apps with minimal download count/reviews but high data exfiltration behavior post-install. Cross-reference app bundle IDs against known legitimate publishers.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Process Activity: Web Scraping Patterns from TV Device
suggestion.rationale: Article states apps perform 'web scraping' for AI training, a behavior divergent from expected smart TV use. Detect process spawning HTTP clients, DOM parsers, or crawler libraries not normally associated with streaming playback or user interface rendering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected process launches (curl, wget, Python requests, Chrome headless modes) originating from third-party TV app processes. Cross-reference against whitelist of legitimate TV services. Flag any process execution from non-system app directories that initiates external HTTP requests.

suggestion.title: Command and Control Traffic Pattern: Tunnel Proxy Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Description of TVs as 'proxies' for external scraping implies C2-like encrypted tunnels or SOCKS proxy establishment. Detect via port usage anomalies, persistent connection establishment to non-standard ports, or process binding to local forwarding ports.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when TV device processes open listening sockets on non-standard ports (1080, 3128, 8080, 9090 for SOCKS/proxy) or establish persistent TCP connections to single external IPs with regular heartbeat traffic, indicating tunnel or proxy channel rather than transient user requests.

suggestion.title: Bulk Content Access Pattern: Simultaneous Requests to Protected Resources
suggestion.rationale: Web scraping for AI training implies systematic enumeration and bulk harvesting of content across multiple domains. Detect via request clustering to login-protected sites, news paywalls, or APIs within short timeframes from single IoT endpoint.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when a smart TV initiates requests to known paywall/authentication-required domains (NY Times, WSJ, banking APIs, pastebin scrapers) in quick succession, or to multiple unrelated domains with identical HTTP headers, indicating automated scraper rather than human user.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Smart TV App Installation from Non-Standard Sources
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'free apps available on Samsung, LG, Roku...have been quietly enrolling millions.' Detect apps installed outside official app stores or with unusual installer origins on TV platforms. Pipeline missed initial access vector entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor TV platform app installation logs for apps deployed outside official Samsung, LG, Roku stores. Flag apps with mismatched signatures, unsigned packages, or installation via sideload mechanisms. Cross-reference app names against official app store catalogs to identify spoofed/repacked variants.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated Consent Dialog Detection in Smart TV Apps
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'consent dialog buried in a TV remote's arrow-key navigation.' Detect apps that hide privacy disclosures in obscured UI states requiring excessive navigation or non-standard input methods to reveal. Missing defense-evasion vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Instrument TV app UI event logging to detect permission dialogs that are buried under >3 menu layers, require non-standard navigation patterns, or use truncated/incomplete consent text. Flag any app requesting network/data permissions with buried or delayed disclosure.

suggestion.title: Smart TV Persistent Outbound Proxy Network Communications
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'enrolled into a commercial residential proxy network' and 'ongoing data scraping.' Apps maintain continuous connections to proxy infrastructure. Detect persistent, repetitive connections to known proxy provider domains/IPs especially with unusual geolocation or bandwidth patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline normal TV network traffic. Alert on apps maintaining persistent connections (>10 min continuous or >5 connections/hour) to known proxy infrastructure (Luminati/Bright Data domains, ASN 62904). Correlate with high volume of unique destination IPs (indicative of proxy rotation) or unexpected geographic exfiltration.

suggestion.title: TV App Auto-Launch and Persistence Mechanisms
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'millions of living room devices into...proxy network' with ongoing activity. Detect apps configured to auto-launch on TV startup or wake, especially with hidden auto-start entries in system configurations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor TV system startup routines and scheduled task configurations for apps registering auto-launch hooks without corresponding user-facing settings. Flag apps that survive TV power-off/on cycles with active network connections before user interaction.

suggestion.title: Web Scraping Activity from Smart TV Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'scrape web data for AI training.' Detect unusual HTTP/HTTPS traffic patterns from TV devices that resemble automated scraping (high request volume to diverse domains, User-Agent anomalies, non-interactive access patterns).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate TV device HTTP requests for high request-to-response ratio, non-human User-Agents, bulk downloads, sequential domain enumeration, and abnormal TLS certificate chains. Scraping typically manifests as >100 requests/hour to diverse domains + high bandwidth on residential IP.

suggestion.title: Repurposed Smart TV Network Device Anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'devices into a commercial residential proxy network.' Detect when TV devices change behavioral baseline: increased outbound connections, new IP destinations, unusual port usage, or acting as intermediary for other network segments.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish TV device network behavior baseline (typical connection count, destination diversity, bandwidth). Alert on sustained deviations: >300% increase in outbound connections, new ASN destinations, or bandwidth utilization >50% of device typical on residential IP without user streaming activity.

suggestion.title: GitHub Repository Unusual Push Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states attack hit '73 Microsoft GitHub Repositories'—the worm propagated by compromising repos, implying abnormal git push/commit operations. No detection logic was suggested despite this being the core attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on GitHub API events showing push/commit operations from IPs or accounts not in baseline (especially from non-Microsoft ASNs), paired with rapid successive commits across multiple repos in short time windows. Cross-correlate with unusual git credential usage (token generation/API key creation) in the same timeframe.

suggestion.title: Worm Self-Replication and Lateral Spread
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly names 'Miasma Worm'—a worm is characterized by self-propagation and lateral movement across repos. No detection logic covers scanning for this behavior (cloning, infection, re-pushing).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unusual git clone operations initiated from a single process/account targeting multiple repositories sequentially, followed by write-back operations (commits). Look for rapid repo enumeration (list/clone calls) within seconds, suggesting automated repo discovery.

suggestion.title: Malware Execution Post-Repository Compromise
suggestion.rationale: A worm hitting repos implies code execution. Pipeline should have surfaced malware execution patterns (process spawning, script execution, binary drop) that occur after repository fetch/clone, but provided no such detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process execution (PowerShell, cmd, bash) spawned shortly after git clone/fetch operations, especially if the process parent is git or a CI/CD runner. Flag if the spawned process writes to unexpected locations, establishes network connections, or injects into running processes.

suggestion.title: Compromised Git Credential or Token Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Worm must have obtained valid credentials or tokens to push changes to 73 repos. No detection rule addresses unusual token generation, credential exposure, or API auth abuse against GitHub.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for PAT (Personal Access Token) or OAuth token creation outside normal admin workflows. Alert on tokens with broad scopes (repo write, delete) created by non-standard accounts or from unusual IPs. Cross-reference with subsequent git operations using those tokens.

suggestion.title: Staged Payload Delivery via GitHub Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attacks often stage malware in GitHub Releases, Actions artifacts, or branches. Article mentions 73 repos compromised but supplies no IOCs—pipeline missed artifact exfiltration or staging detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag downloads of binary or script files from GitHub.com/releases or raw.githubusercontent.com that target non-Microsoft organizational accounts or external hosts. Look for staged files with suspicious names or low-prevalence file hashes.

suggestion.title: GitHub Repository Mass State Change Event
suggestion.rationale: Article states '72 Other Repositories Disabled After Supply Chain Attack'—a coordinated disabling of 73+ repos is a clear high-confidence impact signal that should trigger detection on GitHub API disable/archive events.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor GitHub organization audit logs for bulk repository disable/archive events within a short window. Correlate with GitHub Actions failures across dependent repos. Alert on >5 repos disabled by same actor/automation within 1 hour.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Azure Functions Action Repository Modification
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'Azure Functions Action' as the compromised supply-chain node—detections should catch unauthorized code commits, workflow changes, or dependency injection into widely-used GitHub Actions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline legitimate maintainers and branches for high-dependency GitHub Actions. Alert on commits from new authors, branch protections being disabled, or workflow file modifications without code review. Track downstream dependency pulls.

suggestion.title: Worm Signature: Miasma Malicious Code Injection
suggestion.rationale: Article titles the threat 'Miasma Worm'—malware analysis should surface file hashes, code signatures, and behavioral patterns (e.g., repo enumeration, mass API calls, exfiltration attempts) if indicators are available.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for Miasma hash signatures or yara rules if available. Monitor GitHub Actions for unusual enumeration of repositories, creation of automated commits, or mass API calls to GitHub/Azure APIs from action execution contexts.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Dependency Compromise: Downstream Repository Activation
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 72 dependent repositories affected—detections should identify when repos pull from a compromised upstream action and execute injected code automatically via CI/CD.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for GitHub Actions workflows that pull from known-compromised upstream actions. Correlate action version pinning changes or uses of 'latest' tag with subsequent unusual process execution or credential theft in GitHub Actions environment.

suggestion.title: GitHub Actions Environment Credential Exfiltration Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Malicious GitHub Actions often exfiltrate secrets or tokens—article does not detail exfil but supply-chain attacks targeting AI agents suggest credential/code access. Detection should catch secrets being read/logged.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for GitHub Actions workflows that read GITHUB_TOKEN, access secrets, or clone private repositories. Alert if tokens are then exfiltrated via HTTP POST to external domains, logged in plaintext, or uploaded to cloud storage.

suggestion.title: Account Recovery Tool Abuse: Email Verification Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'HTS didn't verify whether email addresses were associated with the targeted Instagram accounts.' This is the vulnerability enabling password resets without proper identity verification.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on password reset requests to account recovery tool where recovery email does not match primary account email or is not verified against the account's registered contact. Flag high-volume reset attempts targeting multiple accounts within short time window.

suggestion.title: Successful Login Post-Password-Reset on 2FA-Disabled Account
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'hijack accounts without two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled.' Detection must correlate unauthorized password resets with immediate logins where 2FA protection is absent.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect logon events immediately following password resets from different IP/geolocation where account has 2FA disabled. Alert on rapid-fire login attempts after reset—indicator of automated account takeover campaign.

suggestion.title: Bulk Sensitive Data Access from Compromised Account
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies attackers could access 'direct messages and communications, social media posts and content (photos, videos, stories), account activity and interaction history.' Pipeline missed exfiltration patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for bulk retrieval of messages, media, contact lists, or activity logs from recently-compromised accounts. Establish per-account baseline for data access; alert on spike in message/media reads post-password-reset.

suggestion.title: Legitimate Service Abuse: Password Reset via AI Support Tool
